summary: For ages 9–11, treat earthquake-resistant design as a full engineering-design cycle, not a single fact: children define the problem with explicit criteria (keep occupants safe, keep the building standing) and constraints (budget, materials, height), then generate multiple building and community solutions, test each under the same shaking, compare them against shared criteria, and iterate. The honest ceiling is that engineering REDUCES and delays impact and buys escape time — it does not make a building or town hazard-proof. Attach a physical mechanism to every feature (inertia for base isolation, low centre of mass for a wide base, triangulation for cross-bracing, counter-sway for a roof damper) and widen beyond the building to the detect→warn→act system of warning sirens, marked evacuation routes and practised drills.
misconceptions: 'You can build a totally earthquake-proof building.' — Engineering reduces and delays damage; the goal is protecting people and buying escape time, not invincibility.

'A stronger/heavier/more rigid building is always safer.' — Rigidity can be worse; flexible frames and base isolation that let a building sway or decouple from the ground often outperform brute stiffness.
'Base isolation means the building is fixed harder to the ground.' — It is the opposite: bearings DECOUPLE the building so the ground can move without dragging the building with it.
'Bigger earthquake magnitude is the only thing that determines damage.' — Distance, ground type, building design and preparedness all shape the actual impact; design targets the impact side.
'Only the building matters.' — Warning systems, evacuation routes and practised drills reduce human impact as much as structural features; mitigation is a system, not just a stronger wall.
'Drills are a waste of time / the plan is obvious.' — Rehearsed evacuation is itself an engineered solution; it measurably cuts casualties when seconds count (esp. tsunamis).

activities.title: Build, shake, fail, and improve: an earthquake-engineering bench
steps: Define the design problem first: write the criteria (occupants stay safe, building stays standing) and constraints (a fixed budget, limited materials, a target height).
Build a tall tower from a palette of features and shake the base; observe how an un-braced frame racks sideways into a leaning parallelogram and topples.

Change ONE feature at a time and re-test under the SAME shake setting used for every trial (for example, the strong shake): add a wide, low base and see whether toppling reduces; add cross-bracing or shear walls and see whether racking is reduced; place the whole tower on base isolators / rollers and apply that same shake, watching the ground slide underneath while the tower lags and sways less.
Record each trial as a row in a comparison grid (survived the strong shake? cost? height kept?) so trade-offs accumulate and are legible at a glance.
Choose a final design and justify it against the criteria and budget by naming an explicit trade-off (for example, 'base isolation survived the strongest shake but costs the most').
activities.insight: The safest building is not the one clamped hardest to the ground; letting a structure sway or decouple from the moving ground (inertia) can outperform brute stiffness in many settings. Each feature counters a specific physical failure, and engineering reduces impact rather than eliminating the hazard.

activities.title: Coastal town: a detect → warn → act evacuation system
steps: Switch to a coastal-town setting and place the pieces of a warning system: a detection buoy/sensor offshore, a warning siren, a marked evacuation route, and a high-ground or vertical-evacuation destination.
Trigger an undersea earthquake and tsunami, then run a timed evacuation and watch how quickly people reach safety.
Change one part of the system (move the route, add a siren, choose vertical evacuation) and re-run the timed evacuation to see the effect on how many reach high ground in time.

Explain in order how the system works: undersea quake detected → sea-level sensors confirm a tsunami wave (the sea may rise or first pull back) → alert reaches people → evacuate to high ground or a tall, strong building, supported by rehearsed community drills.
activities.insight: Reducing human impact is a system — detect, warn, act — not just a stronger wall; rehearsed evacuation and clear routes save time when seconds count, and a tsunami warning is distinct from feeling the earthquake itself — though near the coast, strong or long shaking is itself a natural warning to move to high ground without waiting for an official alert.

activities.title: Rotate the tower in 3D: watch it sway, topple, and decouple
steps: Rotate a 3D model of a built tower to view it from any angle, then apply shaking and watch it sway and collapse in depth rather than only side-on.
Compare an un-braced frame racking in three dimensions with a braced or base-isolated tower that holds its shape or decouples from the ground.
View a 3D base-isolation cutaway: watch the bearings let the ground slide beneath while the building lags behind in space (inertia).
activities.insight: Toppling, centre of mass, racking and decoupling are spatial; rotating a 3D model can make the direction of sway and the ground-building decoupling easier to see than a flat side-on view.

activities.title: Anatomy of a safe building (reference primer)
steps: Before building, explore a labelled cutaway of an earthquake-resistant building and reveal, one part at a time, what the base isolators, shear walls/cross-bracing, wide base, and roof damper each do.

For each feature, state the physical failure it counters: base isolation decouples the building so the ground can move without dragging it (inertia); wide base and low centre of mass resist toppling; triangulated bracing/shear walls stop racking; a heavy roof damper counter-sways.
Study a base-isolation cutaway showing an arrow for the ground sliding while the building lags behind it.
activities.insight: Each visible feature exists to counter a specific force, and base isolation works by decoupling — the opposite of fixing the building harder to the ground.

activities.title: Talk with an engineer: what is worth the cost?
steps: After iterating on the bench, discuss with someone in the role of a structural/earthquake engineer why tall buildings are allowed to sway, why base isolation works, and how real cities weigh cost against safety.
Pose and answer 'reduce, not eliminate' questions: what does each feature buy, and why can no realistic building be made fully hazard-proof?
Explain back which real trade-offs you would accept and why, connecting the bench's comparison grid to real decisions.
activities.insight: Real hazard engineering is a judgement about reducing impact and buying time within cost limits, not achieving invincibility.

activities.title: Consolidation checks: match mechanisms and order the chain
steps: Match each structural feature to the force or failure it counters (base isolation ↔ ground motion/inertia; cross-bracing ↔ racking; wide/low base ↔ toppling; roof damper ↔ sway).
Put the evacuation steps in order: detect → warn → act (quake detected → sea-level sensors → siren/alert → evacuate to high ground).
Given a shaking scenario, choose which redesign best meets stated criteria and set a cost/safety trade-off, explaining the reasoning.
State in your own words why the goal is reduced impact rather than a hazard-proof building.
activities.insight: A learner can show they recognise the mechanisms, the system ordering, and the 'reduce not eliminate' idea.

checkQuestion: Here are building materials and a tray you can shake like an earthquake. Build a tower that can survive the shaking, then test it, improve it, and show me which changes helped — and tell me how a coastal town would get warning of a tsunami and what people would do.
checkAnswer: The child builds and shake-tests a tower, then improves it with a real earthquake-resistant feature (wide/heavy base, cross-bracing, or a flexible base-isolated foundation) and shows from the re-test that it now sways or survives better; and explains a tsunami warning system detects the undersea quake and rising sea and alerts people to evacuate to high ground, with communities preparing via drills and evacuation routes.
